section_1.title: Prerequisite Visualization: The Cross-Section
section_1.content: Briefly review the definition of a sphere and how a plane intersecting a sphere creates a circular cross-section. Use an animation of a flat slice moving through a ball to establish the concept of 'projected width'.
section_1.example: Imagine a flashlight shining on a basketball; the shadow cast on a wall is a perfect circle.

section_2.title: The Projection Principle: Orthographic Shadows
section_2.content: Explain that when parallel light rays hit a sphere, the shadow cast (the projection) is a circle with the same radius as the sphere. Introduce the formula for the area of this circle: A_shadow = πr².
section_2.example: Use a 3D model of a glowing orange held in front of a whiteboard; notice how regardless of which way the orange is turned, the circular shadow remains constant.

section_3.title: Linking Shadow to Surface Area
section_3.content: Introduce Archimedes' Hat-Box Theorem. Geometrically demonstrate that the surface area of a sphere (4πr²) is exactly four times the area of its projected shadow (πr²).
section_3.example: Visualize a cylinder wrapped around the sphere; the 'lateral area' of the cylinder segment is equal to the 'surface area' of the sphere within that segment.

section_4.title: Application: The Solar Power Challenge
section_4.content: Apply the knowledge to a real-world scenario. Explain why calculating the shadow (cross-section) is crucial for understanding how much energy a spherical object (like a satellite) intercepts from the sun versus its total surface area.
section_4.example: A futuristic space-bot with a spherical solar battery: It only 'sees' the sun through its projected circular area, even though its surface area is much larger.

section_5.title: Summary & Key Takeaway
section_5.content: Recap: Shadow = πr²; Surface Area = 4 × Shadow. Emphasize that the projection is a 2D constraint on a 3D volume.
section_5.example: A final visual showing 4 circular shadows filling the 'unrolled' skin of a sphere, solidifying the 4:1 ratio.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
